title: Written and oral
hookLine: tradition holds Moses received a written Torah and an oral teaching that explains it

lines: HOW MANY TORAHS DO YOU HAVE?
cards: A man who wants to become a Jew comes to the sage Shammai with a question. How many Torahs do you have? Two, says Shammai: a written Torah and an oral Torah.
The man says: the written one I'll believe. The oral one, no. Teach me only the written.
Shammai rebukes him and sends him away. So the man goes to Hillel with the same condition, and Hillel takes him in. The story is in the Talmud, in tractate Shabbat.
What Hillel does on the first two days of lessons is today's word.

teach.h: THE TORAH THAT IS ON THE MOUTH.
teach.b: Torah she-be'al peh. The Torah that is on the mouth: the oral Torah.
Jewish tradition holds that at Sinai Moses received two things together: the written Torah, the five books on the scroll, and a spoken teaching that explains it, passed from teacher to student.
Here's why tradition says the written needs it.

teach.h: BIND THEM? HOW? THE SCROLL IS SILENT.
teach.b: Take one verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." Bind what? How?
What are frontlets? The scroll doesn't say. The answer Jews live by, small black leather boxes holding handwritten verses, tied on with straps, the tefillin, comes from the oral teaching.
Without it, the verse is a beautiful sentence nobody knows how to do. Back to Hillel.

On the first day, he teaches his new student the alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, dalet. The next day, he reads the same letters in the opposite order. The man protests: yesterday you didn't say it that way!

teach.h: WHO TOLD YOU WHICH LETTER WAS ALEF?
teach.b: And Hillel answers, in paraphrase: and how did you know yesterday which letter was alef? You trusted me. Trust me about the oral teaching too.
Even reading the scroll already depends on a voice telling you what the marks are called.
The written gives the words. The spoken gives them a way to be lived.

how: Rabbinic Judaism reads the written Torah through the oral tradition preserved in the Mishnah and Talmud; practices such as tefillin follow that tradition's explanation of the verses. Some Jewish groups, such as the Karaites, read the written Torah without the rabbinic oral tradition.

o: the oral teaching that explains how to live the written Torah
a prayer said aloud instead of reading from a scroll
the Torah read aloud from the scroll in synagogue

games.q: written and oral — tap the pairs.
p: rebuked him and sent him away

s: the written Torah explains exactly how to make tefillin
the verse says bind them for a sign and frontlets between thine eyes. the boxes and straps come from the oral teaching.
in the story, Shammai says there are two Torahs, written and oral
Shammai answers two, written and oral, and Hillel then teaches the man to trust the spoken teaching.
Hillel taught the alphabet the same way both days
on the second day he read the letters in the opposite order, to show the man he'd been trusting a teacher all along.

games.q: you're Hillel. a man wants to join the Jewish people but will accept only the written Torah, not the oral. Shammai has already sent him away. what do you do?
o: take him in and start teaching him the alphabet.
make him accept the oral Torah before you teach him anything.
games.why: Hillel takes him in, then shows him with the alphabet that even reading the written depends on a teacher's voice.

practice: Pick a rule you live by that nobody ever wrote down: how your family sets the table, a habit at work, the right way to fold something.
Explain it quietly out loud, as if to someone who has never seen it done, and notice what you add that no rulebook ever said. If someone's nearby, explain it to them instead.

wordCard.voice: Torah she-be'al peh. The Torah on the mouth: the spoken teaching that, Jewish tradition holds, came with the written Torah and explains how to live it. Today's word.
